detail.title: Linear Regression: Airline Costs
detail.description: Use the Airline Costs dataset (OA 8.4). Predict the number of customers each airline serves from its length of flight and daily flight time per plane. Next, build another regression model to predict the total assets of an airline from the customers served. Do you have any insight about the data from the last two regression models?
detail.understand: Two models: one with two predictors, one with a single predictor. Report each in words: what a one-unit change goes with, how much variation is explained, and which predictors matter.

questions.prompt: Model 1: customers served ~ length of flight + daily flight time.
What insight do the two models give?

detail.interpretation: Flight length, not daily flight time, carries the first model; the second shows that bigger airlines (more customers) have more assets. Both are associations in a small, old sample.
common_mistakes: Reading the coefficient of daily flight time as meaningful when its p-value is large.
Concluding that serving more customers causes higher assets.
Forgetting the units: customers in 1000s, assets in $100,000s.
detail.python_code:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
spans = [(0, 20), (21, 28), (29, 36), (37, 44), (45, 52), (53, 60), (61, 68), (69, 76), (77, 84), (85, 92), (93, 100), (101, 108)]
names = ["airline", "length", "speed", "daily_time", "customers", "op_cost", "rev_tons", "load", "capacity", "assets", "investments", "adj_assets"]
air = pd.read_fwf("airline_costs.dat", colspecs=spans, names=names)

def ols(X, y):
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(y)), X])
    beta = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)[0]
    r2 = 1 - ((y - X @ beta) ** 2).sum() / ((y - y.mean()) ** 2).sum()
    return beta, r2

print(ols(air[["length", "daily_time"]].to_numpy(float), air["customers"].to_numpy(float)))
print(ols(air[["customers"]].to_numpy(float), air["assets"].to_numpy(float)))
notes: Data: Proctor & Duncan (1954) via L. Winner (UF), the file named in OA 8.4. The original URL has moved, so the file comes from the Internet Archive snapshot of that URL (2018-03-25).
The file's column is 'population served (1000s)'; the book's problem calls it 'customers served in 1000s'.

answers.explanation: customers (1000s) = -7792.1 + 183.30·length (miles) -213.3·daily flight time (h); R² = 0.622, adjusted 0.595, F = 23.0. Length: significant (p < 0.001). Daily flight time: not significant (p = 0.88).
total assets ($100,000s) = -98.5 + 0.0217·customers (1000s); R² = 0.819: each extra 1,000 customers goes with about $2,165 more assets.

answers.answer: Airlines with longer flights serve more customers: each extra mile of average flight length goes with about 183 thousand more customers, significant (p < 0.001), while daily flight time adds nothing once length is known (not significant (p = 0.88)); the model explains 62% of the variation. Airlines that serve more customers also hold more assets (82% explained): size goes with size. These are associations among 31 airlines in the early 1950s, not causes, and a few large carriers carry much of the second fit.
